articles.title: Bankers' Books Evidence Act 2026 to come into force from October 1
articles.summary:
Bankers' Books Evidence Act, 2026 which got assent of the President of India last month, and is aimed at providing a modern framework for the use of banking records as evidence in line with contemporary banking practices, will come into force from October 1.
The notification dated September 10 appoints October 1, 2026 as the date on which provisions of the Act will come into force, the finance ministry said in a statement on Friday.
The Act adopts a technology-neutral approach by recognising banking records maintained in physical, electronic, digital, virtual, cloud-based and other contemporary forms, it said.
It also provides for simplified and standardised certification of banking records, including through manual, digital or electronic signatures.
Greater clarity has also been provided on the summoning of bank officials where the bank is not a party to the proceedings, with a "special cause" to be recorded in writing by the court for such summoning, it said.

articles.title: Alembic Pharma clears USFDA inspection at Vadodara bioequivalence facility
articles.summary:
Alembic Pharmaceuticals on Friday said the US health regulator has completed an unannounced inspection at its bioequivalence facility in Vadodara, Gujarat, with zero observation.
In a regulatory filing, the company said the United States Food and Drug Administration (USFDA) carried out the onsite bioequivalence inspection from August 31, 2026, to September 10, 2026.
The inspection concluded with no Form 483 observations, it added.
In USFDA parlance, an FDA Form 483 is issued to a firm's management at the conclusion of an inspection when investigators observe conditions that may violate the Food, Drug, and Cosmetic Act and related regulations. No observations under this rule indicate a clean outcome.

articles.title: Canada work permit delays rise in August
articles.summary: Canada’s processing time for Labour Market Impact Assessments (LMIAs) jumped sharply in August, with employers waiting an average of 156 days for the permanent resident stream, up from 86 days in July. The latest figures from Employment and Social Development Canada (ESDC), released on September 10, show that processing times increased in most Temporary Foreign Worker Program (TFWP) streams.Permanent resident stream sees biggest riseThe permanent resident stream recorded the biggest increase, with the average wait rising by 70 days in one month. The low-wage stream also saw a notable increase, with processing time going up from 73 days in July to 82 days in August.Also Read: Indians can visit UAE to seek jobs without a local employer or sponsor: What you need to knowFor the high-wage stream, the wait increased from 88 days to 90 days. The agricultural stream rose from 23 days to 25 days. The Global Talent Stream remained unchanged at 10 days. This means it continued to meet ESDC’s 10-day service standard.The Seasonal Agricultural Worker Program was the only stream where processing became faster. Its average wait fell from eight days to six days.What the LMIA wait times meanAn LMIA is generally needed when a Canadian employer wants to hire a temporary foreign worker through the TFWP.The assessment checks whether the employer made efforts to find a Canadian citizen or permanent resident for the job and whether hiring a foreign worker could affect the Canadian labour market.Also Read: Trump’s H-1B crackdown hurts Indian IT, but the industry saw it comingThe processing times published by ESDC show the average number of business days needed to assess an application. They do not include the advertising period that employers must complete before applying. Depending on the stream, this can take between 14 days and eight weeks.Canada is also reducing temporary worker numbersThe increase in LMIA processing times comes as Canada continues to reduce the number of temporary foreign workers it plans to admit.The government has set a target of 60,000 TFWP admissions in 2026, down from 82,000 in 2025.In the first half of 2026, 23,190 temporary foreign workers entered Canada. That was 42.1% lower than the number recorded during the same period in 2025.Low-wage LMIA applications also face restrictions in regions where the unemployment rate is 6% or higher. The federal government updates the list of affected regions every quarter.
